newsitem.title: USA: Republicans seek independent counsel for Clinton fund raising.
newsitem.headline: Republicans seek independent counsel for Clinton fund raising.

text.p: Republican leaders said Sunday they want a special counsel to investigate the White House fund raising operation that included apparently unprecedented efforts by Vice President Al Gore.

Senate Majority Whip Don Nickles said he would call on Attorney General Janet Reno on Monday to appoint a special counsel "because I think there are covered persons, including the president, the vice president, the head of the Democratic National Committee, who quite likely have broken the law."
The White House declined immediate comment on a Washington Post story Sunday that Gore directly solicited over $40 million for the 1996 campaign.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said Reno should have already started an investigation as a prelude to the indepdendent counsel, saying she had no other choice.
"I'm wondering why she was resisting this call," he said on ABC Television's "This Week" programme.
"I don't see how she could have avoided starting the preliminary investigation," which he called "totally indefensible."
"I'm not calling for her to step down; I'm calling for her to exercise the law and appoint an independent counsel. I really think she has no choice. I think it's a matter of time."
Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, joined by ranking Democrat Daniel Moynihan, both said they supported an independent counsel on NBC Television's "Meet the Press."
They also agreed that the Senate should give Senator Fred Thompson the $6 million he says is needed to investigate the campaign financing that included possibly illegal donations from abroad.
"Frankly, I think it's time to start backing him and I get a little upset at the way some of our colleagues are trying to thwart this particularr investigation," Hatch said.
Appearing on Fox News Sunday with Nickles, Democrat Bob Torricelli criticised the White House.

"I'm not going to be in the business of defending the undefendable," he said. "And what is more, I do not personally believe it is appropriate for the president or vice president of the United States to directly solicit contributions through telephone calls."
The Post said that Gore telephoned to thank a Texas telecommunications executive after his firm gave $100,000 to the DNC.
It said the contribution was intended in part as a reward to the administration for its efforts to help the firm win a $36 million telecommunications contract in Mexico.
The Post said Gore became known at the Democratic National Committee as the administration's "soliciter-in-chief."
A 1995 memo from a Clinton aide surfaced last week that gave Clinton the names of 10 Democratic donors and ways to encourage contributors with White House perks.
A handwritten addition from Clinton said "ready to start overnight stays right away" and added that other names should be added of donors giving "dollars of "100,000 or more, 50,000 or more."
The White House has steadfastly denied any illegalities.
On Friday, Democratic National Committee officials announced the party was returning another $1.5 million in illegal or questionable donations, bringing to $3 million the amount returned.
